drills.q: A build running directly on the Jenkins controller (as a shortcut, no dedicated agent configured) gets compromised via a malicious dependency. Why is the blast radius worse than if it had happened on a dynamic Kubernetes agent?
drills.a: The controller typically holds credentials (via the Credentials plugin) for every pipeline's deploy targets, so compromising a build there can compromise everything every pipeline has access to. A dynamic agent only holds whatever credentials were explicitly injected for that specific build/stage and is torn down afterward, giving a much smaller blast radius.

drills.q: A pipeline step throws a NotSerializableException-flavored error, but the exact same Groovy code runs fine as a standalone script outside Jenkins. Diagnose and give two possible fixes.
drills.a: Jenkins pipelines run inside a Groovy CPS sandbox so execution state can be serialized to disk and survive controller restarts; some Groovy constructs (certain closures, non-CPS-transformable library calls) don't survive that transformation. Fix: mark the offending method @NonCPS (loses pause/resume durability for that method), or move the logic into a shared library's src/ classes structured around the constraint.

drills.q: A team notices their Jenkinsfile hasn't changed but a build starts failing differently than before. What's a likely shared-library-related cause?
drills.a: An unpinned @Library reference (e.g. @Library('lib@master')) picked up a new commit merged to the shared library's default branch, silently changing pipeline behavior. Fix: pin @Library references to specific, immutable tags.

drills.q: Builds are stuck Pending in the Jenkins queue, but every agent's Grafana dashboard shows plenty of free CPU and memory. What should you check next, and why wouldn't just raising a number blindly be the right fix?
drills.a: Check the executor count configured per agent in the build queue view — it's a distinct concurrency constraint from raw resource capacity. Raising executor count too high without matching real resource headroom just moves the bottleneck from 'queued and waiting' to 'running but starved,' which is often harder to diagnose since builds appear to be progressing.

drills.q: A build passes reliably on one static Jenkins agent and fails intermittently on another agent with an identical configuration. What's the likely cause and the structural fix?
drills.a: State bleed from a previous build on the long-lived static agent — cached dependencies, leftover processes, or disk artifacts from an earlier build. The structural fix is migrating to dynamic Kubernetes agents that spin up a fresh pod per build with no persisted state, rather than adding ad hoc cleanup steps to static agents.

drills.q: A script authenticating correctly against the Jenkins REST API still gets a 403 on a POST request. The same credentials work fine for GET requests. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: A missing CSRF crumb token — Jenkins requires it by default on state-changing (POST/PUT/DELETE-style) requests but not on read-only GET requests, which explains why GETs succeed and the state-changing call fails with what looks like a permissions error. Fetch a crumb from the crumb issuer endpoint and include it on the request.

drills.q: A new startup building entirely on GitHub with no special compliance requirements asks whether they should set up Jenkins or use GitHub Actions. What's the honest recommendation, and what would change your answer?
drills.a: GitHub Actions — zero infrastructure to patch and secure, no plugin-CVE surface to manage, and tight native integration for a team with normal compliance needs. The answer would change toward Jenkins if they had genuine air-gapped/on-prem requirements, needed deep customization via specific plugins with no hosted equivalent, or already had complex multi-repo orchestration built up that would be costly to re-architect.

drills.q: A security review finds a Jenkins controller with 60 installed plugins, several flagged with known CVEs, and nobody sure why half of them are installed. What's the correct remediation approach, and why isn't 'just remove all unused plugins once' sufficient long-term?
drills.a: Audit installed plugins against actual usage, remove unused ones, and track CVEs against the versions of what remains, restricting who can install new plugins going forward. A one-time cleanup isn't sufficient because a plugin safe at install time can develop a vulnerability or go unmaintained later — this requires ongoing inventory and CVE-tracking discipline, not a single pass.
